exercises.prompt:
What value does this expression have?

```scheme
(* (+ 2 3) (- 10 (/ 12 4)))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Evaluate the innermost call first: what is `(/ 12 4)`, and what is 10 minus that?

exercises.solution: It is **35**. The operands of `*` are `(+ 2 3)`, which is 5, and `(- 10 (/ 12 4))`, which is `(- 10 3)`, or 7. Multiplying gives 35.

feedback.message: Not yet. Both 6 and 4 are exact integers. Does Scheme turn the answer into a floating-point number?
Not yet. That is what `quotient` would give. `/` keeps the exact answer.
Close. Scheme always reduces rationals to lowest terms.

hints: Exact divided by exact stays exact, reduced to lowest terms.
exercises.solution: It prints **`3/2`**. Dividing two exact integers gives an exact rational, automatically reduced. To get 1.5, make an operand inexact (`(/ 6.0 4)`) or call `(inexact (/ 6 4))`.

exercises.prompt: Which of these values counts as false in a Scheme `if`?

options.label: `#f` only
options.feedback: Yes. In Scheme every value except `#f` counts as true.

options.label: `#f` and the empty list `'()`
options.feedback: Not yet. Some older Lisps treated the empty list as false, but Scheme does not: `(if '() 'yes 'no)` is `yes`.

options.label: `#f`, `0` and the empty string
options.feedback: Not yet. That is closer to C or Python. In Scheme, 0 and `""` are true.

options.label: Nothing: `if` only accepts booleans.
options.feedback: Not yet. `if` accepts any value as its test.

hints: Scheme has exactly one false value.
exercises.solution: **Only `#f`** is false. Everything else, including `'()`, `0` and `""`, is true. To test for an empty list, use `(null? lst)`; for zero, `(zero? n)`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print? Type the line exactly.

```scheme
(import (scheme base) (scheme write))
(write "hi") (display "hi") (newline)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `write` prints a string the way you would type it in code. What does that include?
Close, but neither procedure adds a space between outputs.

hints: `write` shows strings with their quotes; `display` shows only the characters.
exercises.solution: It prints **`"hi"hi`**. `write` prints the string as Scheme source, with quotes; `display` prints just its characters. Nothing adds a space between them.

feedback.message: Not yet. That is `(modulo -7 3)`, which takes the sign of the divisor. `remainder` takes the sign of the dividend.
Not yet. Check the sign: `remainder` keeps the sign of -7.

exercises.solution: It is **-1**. `quotient` truncates toward zero, so `(quotient -7 3)` is -2, and -7 = 3 × (-2) + (-1). `modulo` instead gives 2, the result with the sign of the divisor. (R7RS also offers `truncate-remainder` and `floor-remainder`, whose names say exactly which rounding they use.)

feedback.message: Not yet. `exact` converts the inexact 0.5 into an exact number. How is an exact one half written?

hints: `exact` turns a floating-point number into an exact rational when it can be represented exactly.
exercises.solution: It prints **`(1/2 0.75)`**. 0.5 is exactly representable in binary floating point, so `exact` gives the rational `1/2`. `inexact` turns the exact 3/4 into the floating-point 0.75.

exercises.prompt: A program file contains only `(import (scheme base))` followed by `(display "hello")`. Running it with `chibi-scheme` fails with "undefined variable: display". Why?

options.label: `display` lives in `(scheme write)`, which the program did not import.
options.feedback: Yes. R7RS programs see only what their imports provide; add `(scheme write)` to the import list.

options.label: Chibi-Scheme does not support `display`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Every R7RS implementation provides `display`, in the `(scheme write)` library.

options.label: Strings must be written with single quotes.
options.feedback: Not yet. Strings use double quotes; a single quote means quotation of data.

options.label: `display` must be called inside a procedure named `main`.
options.feedback: Not yet. A Scheme program is just a sequence of top-level forms; there is no required `main`.

hints: Which library did the lesson say provides `display` and `write`?
exercises.solution: **`display` comes from `(scheme write)`.** Change the first line to `(import (scheme base) (scheme write))`. The REPL loads the whole standard by default, which is why the same expression works when typed interactively.

exercises.prompt: Which Scheme standard does this course follow, and when was it completed?

options.label: R7RS-small, completed in 2013
options.feedback: Yes. It returned to Scheme's minimalist tradition and added a simple library system.

options.label: R5RS, completed in 1998
options.feedback: Not yet. R5RS was the long-time baseline, but R7RS-small replaced it.

options.label: R6RS, completed in 2007
options.feedback: Not yet. R6RS is a much larger language; some implementations, such as Chez Scheme, follow it, but this course uses R7RS-small.

options.label: ANSI Common Lisp, 1994
options.feedback: Not yet. Common Lisp is a different member of the Lisp family, with its own standard.

hints: Look at the `import` line at the top of every program in the course.
exercises.solution: **R7RS-small (2013).** It is the current Scheme standard, small enough to read in full, and supported by implementations such as Chibi-Scheme, Gauche, Guile 3 and CHICKEN (with its r7rs extension). Work on the larger R7RS-large language continues.
